title: Cybernetics, interoception, and the art of embodiment - Nature Machine Intelligence
text:
Download PDF

Living organisms continuously monitor their internal physiological states while interacting with complex environments and adapt their actions in response to changes in these internal signals. New work combines such biological principles with cybernetics, reinforcement learning and neuroscience to develop a framework for autonomous and adaptive artificial embodied agents.

In the 1940s, Norbert Wiener developed cybernetics, an approach that emphasized the central role of feedback loops in both intelligent life and machines1. For biological agents, survival depends on effective monitoring and regulation of internal states such as body temperature, oxygen levels or blood glucose. Keeping these within healthy ranges while interacting with a complex environment motivates behaviours and actions. Wiener recognized such feedback, control and action loops all around him and successfully used these principles in engineering applications, helping to establish cybernetics as a framework to understand both natural and artificial systems.Despite Wiener’s success in applying cybernetic principles, the theory was largely ignored when artificial intelligence (AI) emerged as a new research direction in the late 1950s. Following the Dartmouth workshop on AI in 1956, which famously launched the field, research focussed on symbolic AI, knowledge representation, reasoning and logical problem solving. Questions of embodiment and self-regulation received comparatively less attention. However, cybernetic approaches have continued to play a part in fields such as robotics, control theory and autonomous systems.In the meantime, the field of AI has given rise to powerful large language models (LLMs) that can solve complex problems and generate human-like text, code, video and more. However, such models typically pursue narrowly defined tasks and operate within well-specified computational environments. Despite recent interest in combining LLMs with physical embodiment, extending their capabilities to support reliable operation in physical environments remains challenging. In the real world, intelligent systems contend with changing conditions, limited resources and constraints on their operation.Sungwoo Lee et al. argue that ideas related to cybernetics could advance the development of modern AI into adaptive and autonomous agents in the physical world. In a Perspective in this issue, they propose a framework that endows embodied AI systems with an internal environment and interoceptive inputs: the ability to monitor internal states and autonomously update goals in response to changes. This approach combines ideas from AI, robotics, neuroscience and cognitive science.In robotics, self-monitoring, or system health monitoring, is a longstanding technique that is particularly important in applications such as space exploration and disaster response, in which careful tracking of signals such as battery status, temperature and strain is essential. The interoceptive framework proposed by Lee et al. formalizes self-monitoring as part of a closed feedback loop, in which environmental conditions alter internal signals that, in turn, shape actions.The framework also builds on earlier reinforcement learning approaches in which internal states act as a source of reward for agents with open-ended goals2. However, Lee et al. extend this idea by modelling internal states not just as rewards but as stable contextual variables that influence learning and decision-making. For example, in living organisms, physiological needs such as hunger or thirst do not just generate rewards, but also alter what information is salient and which behaviours are prioritized.Lee et al. argue that similar mechanisms could help embodied artificial agents function in changing environments by using internal states to tune policy selection, exploration strategies and memory updating. In this formulation, interoception is not merely a mechanism to monitor and regulate internal states, but also a computational link between those states and adaptive behaviour. Their relative stability may provide a reference signal that helps agents adapt in non-stationary environments.Future work will need to demonstrate whether the proposed framework can be of practical use in advancing robotics and physical AI, but the ideas are thought-provoking. In our April Editorial, we wrote that several frameworks are converging on the scientific question of what it takes for a system not just to predict, simulate or reason about the world, but to act intelligently and physically within it. The interoceptive AI framework proposed by Lee et al. advances this effort by incorporating biologically grounded internal states into AI systems. In doing so, the Perspective highlights the continuing relevance of cybernetic ideas as AI systems move beyond modelling the world to acting within it.
